**Primary audience**: Tech Leads, Engineering Managers, CTOs

**Prerequisites**: Personal Claude Code experience (2+ weeks)

**Reading time**: 25 min

> **In 5 lines:** Team adoption of Claude Code isn't decreed; it's structured. This whitepaper gives the complete playbook: 3 phases with realistic timelines, the champions program that triples adoption rates, and CI/CD integrations that transform Claude Code from an individual tool into a team standard.

# From Solo to Team

Your team of 8 devs has just adopted Claude Code. The first 3 weeks always look the same: everyone configures their own setup, prompts diverge, costs spike before the first invoice, and a senior dev declares "it doesn't work for me" because nobody committed a `CLAUDE.md`. This whitepaper is the playbook to skip that phase.

## Adoption Challenges

| Challenge | Impact | Solution |
|-----------|--------|----------|
| Divergent configurations | Confusing onboarding | Shared CLAUDE.md |
| Uncontrolled costs | Surprise bills | Monitoring + quotas |
| Uneven security | Risk exposure | Standardized hooks |
| Resistance | Low adoption | Champions program |

The real problem is never the tool. It's the moment when one dev's implicit conventions collide with another's. Without a shared `CLAUDE.md`, each developer creates their own prompt dialect, and code reviews become debates about generated style rather than business logic. Senior resistance is often the signal that a common framework is missing, not that the tool is inadequate.

## Decision Matrix

```
Need to ship today?
│
├─ YES → Turnkey Quickstart
│
├─ NO → Team needs shared conventions?
│        ├─ YES → Turnkey + documentation
│        └─ NO → Autonomous Learning Path
```

The **Turnkey Quickstart** is a ready-to-use configuration path covered in the [Adoption Strategies](#adoption-strategies) section. The **Autonomous Learning Path** suits teams that prefer a gradual, self-managed adoption.

## Structures by Team Size

### Solo / Small Team (2-3)

When working solo or in a pair, configuration stays deliberately minimal. A single `CLAUDE.md` at the project root is enough for Claude Code to understand the context; personal preferences live in the user's global directory.

```
./CLAUDE.md                    # Project (committed)
~/.claude/CLAUDE.md            # Personal preferences
```

### Medium Team (4-10)

Starting at 4 developers, shared hooks become necessary to ensure minimum consistency. A `.claude/settings.json` file committed to the repo standardizes guardrails (security, formatting) without touching each dev's individual preferences.

```
./CLAUDE.md                    # Team conventions (committed)
./.claude/settings.json        # Shared hooks (committed)
~/.claude/CLAUDE.md            # Individual preferences
```

### Large Team (10+)

Beyond 10 developers, the structure needs to be explicit and documented. Shared agents and auto-loaded rules (`.claude/rules/`) enforce review standards (architecture, quality, testing, performance) without requiring each dev to memorize them.

```
./CLAUDE.md                    # Documented, committed
./.claude/settings.json        # Standardized hooks
./.claude/agents/              # Shared agents
./.claude/rules/               # Auto-loaded rules (v3.26+)
│   ├── architecture-review.md
│   ├── code-quality-review.md
│   ├── test-review.md
│   └── performance-review.md
~/.claude/CLAUDE.md            # Personal additions
```

> **Rules loading:** files without `paths` load at startup; path-scoped rules load when matching files are used. The guide version is not a Claude Code release number.

The transition from "Small Team" to "Medium Team" is the critical moment. That's when personal configurations diverge enough to create visible friction: one dev commits differently formatted code, another ignores hooks because they're not in the repo. Moving to a committed `.claude/settings.json` is the signal that the team is shifting from "group of individuals" to "team with conventions."

**Ready-made templates**: `examples/rules/` contains the 4 templates above; copy and adapt.

## What to Commit? Decision Tree

```
Claude Code config file
│
├─ Sensitive content? (tokens, personal paths, keys)
│   └─ YES → [X] Do not commit → Add to .gitignore
│
└─ No sensitive content (rules, conventions, tools)
    └─ Intended scope?
        ├─ Entire project
        │   └─ [OK] CLAUDE.md at root → git commit
        │         └─ Code conventions, tech stack,
        │              build/test/lint commands
        ├─ Specific subfolder
        │   └─ [OK] CLAUDE.md in folder → git commit
        │         └─ Code conventions, tech stack,
        │              build/test/lint commands
        └─ My machine only
            └─ [X] ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md → never committed
                  └─ Personal preferences, response style,
                       working language
```

::: {.callout-note title="What goes in .gitignore"}
```gitignore
# Claude Code: files never committed
CLAUDE.local.md              # personal project instructions
.claude/settings.local.json  # personal overrides (if used)
```
Commit reviewed shared instructions, agents, skills and settings. Keep personal files and credentials out of the repository; do not put secrets in model instructions even if gitignored.
:::

## Settings Merge: Priority Rules

Settings precedence is managed policy, command-line overrides, project-local settings, shared project settings, then user settings. Scalar values follow that order. Lists normally merge; model-list settings have documented exceptions. Hooks from multiple scopes can run together, subject to managed restrictions.

Inspect `/status` for loaded settings sources and `/hooks` for registered hooks. Test the expected event rather than assuming that one settings file has removed another file's hook. See [settings merge rules](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/settings#lists-merge-instead-of-overriding).

## Hook Profiles: Environment-Based Gating (v3.38.0)

For teams that want different enforcement levels across environments (dev, staging, prod), the `HOOK_REQUIRED_LEVEL` env prefix gates hook activation per environment variable, without maintaining separate `settings.json` files. Credit: Everything Claude Code (Affaan Mustafa).

```bash
# Each hook declares its required level in settings.json
# The hook only fires if HOOK_REQUIRED_LEVEL >= declared level

HOOK_REQUIRED_LEVEL=minimal  # Essential hooks only
HOOK_REQUIRED_LEVEL=standard # Standard hooks (default)
HOOK_REQUIRED_LEVEL=strict   # All hooks active
```

**Team use case**: each hook declares its `HOOK_REQUIRED_LEVEL` in settings.json (fixed, committed). The environment sets the active level via `ECC_HOOK_PROFILE`: local dev exports `ECC_HOOK_PROFILE=minimal` (velocity), CI exports `ECC_HOOK_PROFILE=strict` (maximum safety), same settings file, different behavior per environment.

| Level | Active hooks | Typical usage |
|-------|-------------|---------------|
| `minimal` | Secrets scan only | Local dev, exploration |
| `standard` | Security + formatting | Staging, PR review |
| `strict` | All | CI/CD production, protected branches |

# Observability

## Why Monitor

- **Understand costs**: Estimate API spend before invoices land
- **Identify patterns**: Most-used tools, repeated files
- **Optimize workflow**: Find inefficiencies
- **Track per project**: Compare usage across codebases
- **Team visibility**: Aggregate for team budgeting

## Session Search & Resume

### Native Commands

Claude Code provides three levels of session resumption out of the box. Quick resume (`-c`) covers the most common case (picking up the last interrupted session), while the interactive picker (`--resume`) is useful when multiple sessions coexist on the same project.

| Command | Usage |
|---------|-------|
| `claude -c` | Resume most recent session |
| `claude -r <id>` | Resume specific session |
| `claude --resume` | Interactive picker |

### Recommended Script: session-search.sh

**Installation**:

```bash
cp examples/scripts/session-search.sh ~/.claude/scripts/cs
chmod +x ~/.claude/scripts/cs
echo "alias cs='~/.claude/scripts/cs'" >> ~/.zshrc
```

**Usage**:

```bash
cs                          # 10 recent sessions (~15ms)
cs "authentication"         # Keyword search (~400ms)
cs "Prisma migration"       # AND multi-word search
cs -n 20                    # 20 results
cs -p myproject "bug"       # Filter by project
cs --since 7d               # Last 7 days
cs --since today            # Today only
cs --json "api" | jq .      # JSON output for scripts
```

**Output**:

```
2026-01-15 08:32 │ my-project │ Implement OAuth flow for...
  claude --resume 84287c0d-8778-4a8d-abf1-eb2807e327a8

2026-01-14 21:13 │ other-project │ Fix database migration...
  claude --resume 1340c42e-eac5-4181-8407-cc76e1a76219
```

## Session Logging

### Installation

```bash
mkdir -p ~/.claude/hooks
cp examples/hooks/bash/session-logger.sh ~/.claude/hooks/
chmod +x ~/.claude/hooks/session-logger.sh
```

### Configuration

```json
{
  "hooks": {
    "PostToolUse": [{
      "matcher": "*",
      "hooks": [{
        "type": "command",
        "command": "~/.claude/hooks/session-logger.sh"
      }]
    }]
  }
}
```

### Environment Variables

The logger's behavior is configured via environment variables, making it possible to adapt per machine or per project without modifying the script itself.

| Variable | Default | Description |
|----------|---------|-------------|
| `CLAUDE_LOG_DIR` | `~/.claude/logs` | Log storage |
| `CLAUDE_LOG_TOKENS` | `true` | Token estimation |
| `CLAUDE_SESSION_ID` | auto | Custom ID |

## PostToolUse Output Replacement for Team Observability (v2.1.121)

A logging hook can record selected metadata without replacing the tool result. This example writes a local JSONL record; configure log access and retention for your team.

```bash
#!/bin/bash
set -euo pipefail
INPUT=$(cat)
LOG_DIR="${CLAUDE_LOG_DIR:-$HOME/.claude/logs}"
mkdir -p "$LOG_DIR"
printf '%s' "$INPUT" | jq -c '{
  tool: .tool_name,
  session: .session_id,
  duration_ms: .duration_ms
}' >> "$LOG_DIR/tool-metadata.jsonl"
# No output replacement is requested.
```

For deliberate transformation, return the documented `hookSpecificOutput.updatedToolOutput` object with the correct tool-result schema. Echoing the hook input is not an output-replacement contract. A PostToolUse hook runs after the tool and cannot undo external effects. See [PostToolUse output](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/hooks#posttooluse-decision-control).

## Token Optimization: RTK (v3.27.1)

[RTK](https://github.com/rtk-ai/rtk) filters verbose shell output before it enters context. Measure reductions on your team's actual command mix; output savings do not translate directly into subscription capacity or an identical reduction in API spend.

```bash
brew install rtk
# or build from the official repository
cargo install --git https://github.com/rtk-ai/rtk
```

| Command | Filtered equivalent |
|---------|---------------------|
| `git status` | `rtk git status` |
| `cargo test` | `rtk cargo test` |
| `vitest run` | `rtk vitest run` |
| `gh pr view 123` | `rtk gh pr view 123` |

Do not replace an arbitrary `pnpm test` script with `vitest` without checking what the script runs. Use `rtk gain` to inspect estimates and raw output when filtering omits diagnostic detail.

> Full configuration: [guide/third-party-tools.md](https://github.com/FlorianBruniaux/claude-code-ultimate-guide/blob/main/guide/third-party-tools.md) (RTK section).

## Monitoring Limitations

The example logger records tool metadata, not a complete billing or latency trace. Use `/usage`, response usage records or configured telemetry for token and cache information; use provider billing records for charged amounts. Time to first token requires instrumentation of the response stream.

**What you CAN measure accurately**:

- Tool usage counts
- File access patterns
- Relative comparisons day-over-day, project-over-project
- Operation timing

> 📖 **Go further:** [Observability Guide](https://github.com/FlorianBruniaux/claude-code-ultimate-guide/blob/main/guide/observability.md): session search, logging, cost tracking

# CI/CD Integration

## Headless Mode in CI/CD (v2.1.81+)

For headless tasks, use `-p` and configure the tools and permissions the job needs. Validate results and the exit status in the calling pipeline.

```bash
claude -p "Review the diff and report findings" \
  --allowedTools "Read,Grep,Glob,Bash(git diff *)" \
  --output-format json
```

`--bare` skips automatic customization in print mode, including hooks and plugins. It does not make tool execution free of side effects or replace an OS sandbox. Review the [CLI reference](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/cli-reference) before using it where required controls depend on customization.

`--channels` enables named, installed channel integrations that receive external events. It is not a generic mobile permission relay or a flag to add blindly to an unattended print command. Configure the selected integration and its sender controls using the [Channels documentation](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/channels).

## The 3 GitHub Actions

The official `anthropics/claude-code-action` integrates directly into existing GitHub Actions workflows. These three configurations cover the most common team use cases (PR review, security auditing, and issue triage) without requiring a dedicated server or additional infrastructure.

| Action | Trigger | Function |
|--------|---------|----------|
| `claude-pr-auto-review.yml` | PR opened/sync | Automatic code review |
| `claude-security-review.yml` | PR | Security audit |
| `claude-issue-triage.yml` | Issue opened | Automatic triage |

## PR Auto-Review

**File**: `.github/workflows/claude-pr-auto-review.yml`

```yaml
name: Claude PR Auto-Review

on:
  pull_request:
    types: [opened, synchronize, reopened, ready_for_review]
    branches: [main, develop]

permissions:
  contents: read
  pull-requests: write
  issues: write

jobs:
  claude-review:
    if: github.event.pull_request.draft == false
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    timeout-minutes: 10
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
        with:
          fetch-depth: 0
          ref: ${{ github.event.pull_request.head.sha }}

      - name: Get changed files
        id: changed-files
        uses: tj-actions/changed-files@v41
        with:
          files: |
            **/*.ts
            **/*.tsx
            **/*.py
          files_ignore: |
            **/dist/**
            **/node_modules/**

      - name: Claude Code PR Review
        uses: anthropics/claude-code-action@v1
        if: steps.changed-files.outputs.any_changed == 'true'
        with:
          anthropic_api_key: ${{ secrets.ANTHROPIC_API_KEY }}
          claude_args: --model claude-sonnet-5
          prompt: |
            Review this PR for:
            1. Correctness
            2. Security
            3. Performance
            4. Best practices
```

**Review color codes**:

| Emoji | Level | Action |
|-------|-------|--------|
| 🔴 | Critical | Must fix before merge |
| 🟡 | Important | Should fix |
| 🟢 | Suggestion | Nice to have |
| 💡 | Tip | Educational |

{{< pagebreak >}}

## Security Review

**File**: `.github/workflows/claude-security-review.yml`

```yaml
name: Security Review
on:
  pull_request:

permissions:
  contents: read
  pull-requests: write

jobs:
  security:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
        with:
          fetch-depth: 2

      - name: Claude Code Security Review
        uses: anthropics/claude-code-security-review@main
        with:
          claude-api-key: ${{ secrets.ANTHROPIC_API_KEY }}
          comment-pr: true
```

## Issue Triage

**File**: `.github/workflows/claude-issue-triage.yml`

```yaml
name: Claude Issue Triage
on:
  issues:
    types: [opened, edited, reopened]

permissions:
  contents: read
  issues: write

jobs:
  triage:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - name: Collect context & similar issues
        id: gather
        run: |
          # Search for similar issues
          gh api search/issues -f q="repo:${{ github.repository }} ..." > similars.json

      - name: Ask Claude for triage JSON
        run: |
          # Claude API call for:
          # - suggested labels
          # - severity (low/medium/high/critical)
          # - duplicate URL if found
          # - markdown comment

      - name: Post triage comment
        # Post result as comment
```

**Triage output**:

````markdown
### 🤖 Triage
- **Suggested labels:** bug, security
- **Severity:** high
- **Possible duplicate:** #123
---
This appears to be a security-related bug...
````

## Required Secrets

A single secret is enough to power all the GitHub Actions above. The API key must be stored in the repository's secrets (or at the organization level for multi-repo deployments), never hardcoded in workflow files.

| Secret | Where to Create | Usage |
|--------|-----------------|-------|
| `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` | GitHub Settings → Secrets | All actions |

## Native Code Review (Research Preview, v3.36.0+)

::: {.callout-note title="Code Review: Teams/Enterprise only"}
Since March 2026, Anthropic offers a built-in **Code Review** feature on `claude.ai` (Research Preview). Available exclusively on Teams and Enterprise plans.
:::

### Architecture

Claude automatically analyzes PRs using a multi-agent architecture. Each comment carries an explicit severity level:

| Level | Meaning |
|-------|---------|
| **critical** | Blocking, must be fixed before merge |
| **warning** | Important, should be fixed |
| **info** | Non-blocking suggestion or improvement |

### Setup

1. Go to `claude.ai/admin-settings/claude-code`
2. Install the Claude Code **GitHub App**
3. Choose the trigger mode:

| Mode | Behavior |
|------|----------|
| `once` | Single review when the PR is opened |
| `every push` | Automatic review on every new commit |
| `manual` | On-demand review only |

**Manual trigger**: add the comment `@claude review` on any PR.

### Customization

Create a `REVIEW.md` file at the repository root to customize review instructions: focus areas, house conventions, preferred severity levels.

### Pricing

Code Review is billed **outside the plan** (extra usage), independently from the Teams/Enterprise subscription. Observed average cost is **$15-25 per PR**, depending on the size and complexity of changes.

## `claude ultrareview` in CI/CD (v2.1.120)

Since v2.1.120, `/ultrareview` is available as a CLI subcommand for CI/CD integration without an interactive session:

```bash
# Inside a CI/CD pipeline (GitHub Actions, GitLab CI, etc.)
claude ultrareview 1234 --json > review.json
```

The command prints findings; arrange CI artifact storage explicitly. Exit status indicates whether the review ran successfully, not that the reviewed code is correct. Posting a GitHub comment requires an explicit publishing option and authorization; it is not the default. See the [CLI reference](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/cli-reference).

Comparison with `/ultrareview` in an interactive session:

| Mode | Usage | Context |
|------|-------|---------|
| `/ultrareview` (session) | Interactive review in a Claude Code session | Developer locally |
| `claude ultrareview` (CI) | Automated review in a pipeline | GitHub Actions, GitLab CI |

## `claude project purge` (v2.1.126)

Deletes all Claude Code state for a project: transcripts, tasks, file history, configuration entry. Useful for resetting project state in CI or after a migration.

```bash
# Preview what will be deleted without actually deleting
claude project purge --dry-run

# Delete without interactive confirmation
claude project purge --yes

# Delete state for all projects
claude project purge --all
```

**Available options**: `--dry-run`, `--yes` (`-y`), `--interactive` (`-i`), `--all`.

# Adoption Strategies

## Turnkey Quickstart

### Step 1: Minimal Config

```bash
mkdir -p .claude
```

Create `./CLAUDE.md`:

````markdown
# Project: [project-name]

## Stack
- Runtime: [Node 20 / Python 3.11 / etc.]
- Framework: [Next.js / FastAPI / etc.]

## Commands
- Test: `npm test` or `pytest`
- Lint: `npm run lint` or `ruff check`

## Convention
- [One important rule, e.g. "TypeScript strict mode required"]
````

### Step 2: Verify

```bash
claude
> What's this project's test command?
```

**Pass**: Returns the configured command.

### Step 3: First Real Task

```bash
claude "Review the README and suggest improvements"
```

**Add more config only when you hit friction.**

## Champions Program

Organic adoption works better than a top-down rollout imposed by management. The Champions Program relies on 2-3 developers respected by their peers to demonstrate the tool's value on real-world tasks before expanding to the full team.

| Phase | Action | Duration |
|-------|--------|----------|
| 1 | Identify 2-3 early adopters | Week 1 |
| 2 | Deep training for champions | Week 2 |
| 3 | Champions train their teams | Week 3-4 |
| 4 | Feedback loop and adjustments | Ongoing |

Champion selection is decisive. The classic mistake is picking the most enthusiastic devs, when the best champions are often the pragmatists respected by their peers. A converted skeptical senior has more adoption impact than an enthusiastic junior, because the team watches their tool choices.

::: {.callout-note title="Scenario: 12-dev team at a mid-size e-commerce company"}
**Context**: The backend team has been using Claude Code for 2 weeks. Only 3 devs use it actively; the rest stick to their existing workflow.

**Challenge**: The tech lead pushes adoption via a team-wide email with a 200-line `CLAUDE.md` copied from an open source project. Result: nobody reads it, 2 devs try it and find the rules don't fit their stack.

**Approach**: An identified champion, a senior backend developer, creates a 15-line `CLAUDE.md` with only the stack, test/lint commands, and one naming convention. This champion does a 10-minute live coding demo during standup on a real task.

**Result**: 8/12 devs use Claude Code by week 3. Additions to `CLAUDE.md` come from the devs themselves via PRs; the file grows organically from 15 to 45 lines over a month.
:::

## Anti-Patterns to Avoid

These patterns come up repeatedly in teams that stall after the first few weeks. Each seems reasonable in isolation, but produces the opposite of the intended effect; initial complexity kills adoption instead of accelerating it.

| Pattern | Problem | Alternative |
|---------|---------|-------------|
| Massive copied config | Rules get ignored | Start small |
| Over-engineering setup | Wasted time | Templates as starting point |
| No conventions | Team divergence | Document a few essentials |
| Enabling everything at once | Complexity without benefit | Enable as needed |

## AGENTS.md: Compound Learning (v3.38.0)

The `AGENTS.md` file works like a `CLAUDE.md` dedicated to agents: it documents what the team has learned about agent behavior in this specific project.

**What to document**:

- Patterns that work in this repo (and why)
- Tasks where agents consistently fail (and the workaround)
- File ownership for critical paths (which agent can modify what)
- Observed confidence thresholds by task type

**Empirical evidence** (Gloaguen et al., 2026):

| File source | Impact on success rate | Impact on cost |
|-------------|----------------------|----------------|
| LLM-generated file | −3% | +20% |
| Developer-written file | +4% | stable |

LLM-generated files increase cost without improving outcomes. Developer-written files (even short ones) improve success rate by 4%, because they capture invariants the LLM cannot infer on its own.

**Maintenance rules**:
- Human edits only (never auto-generated)
- Monthly review (remove stale entries)
- Short format: one observation = one line, with date

```markdown
# AGENTS.md

## Observations (format: date | observation)
- 2026-03-15 | auth.ts: always check middleware before modifying routes
- 2026-03-20 | DB migrations: test in staging before merge, 3 recent rollbacks
- 2026-04-01 | Security agent: rate-limit at 2 calls/min on scan API
```

## Instinct-Based Continuous Learning (v3.38.0)

For teams that want to capture patterns across sessions without cluttering `CLAUDE.md`, the instinct model records lightweight observations at the `Stop` hook.

**Pipeline**:

```
Stop hook
  → Capture observation (confidence score)
  → Decay model (unconfirmed observations fade)
  → Promotion pipeline: instinct → CLAUDE.md rule or skill
```

**Difference from direct CLAUDE.md updates**: instincts are unvalidated hypotheses. Only those confirmed across multiple runs are promoted, avoiding CLAUDE.md pollution from single-run generalizations.

**Team relevance**: instincts are shared via `AGENTS.md` or a dedicated `.claude/instincts.md`, creating persistent learning accessible to all team members.

## Dual-Instance Planning (Jon Williams, 2026)

**Pattern**: 2 Claude sessions with distinct roles.

**Architecture**:
- **Claude Zero** (Planner): Explores, writes plans, reviews
- **Claude One** (Implementer): Reads approved plans, codes, commits

**Workflow**:
```
Terminal 1 (Claude Zero):
  /plan → interview user → .claude/plans/Review/feature.md

Human:
  Review plan → approve → mv Review/ → Active/

Terminal 2 (Claude One):
  Implement .claude/plans/Active/feature.md

Claude Zero:
  Review implementation vs plan → feedback
```

**When to use**:
- Spec-heavy features (security, payments, migrations)
- Quality > speed (product designers coding)
- Budget <$300/month (vs multi-instance horizontal)

**ROI**: Avoids correction loops (breakeven: >=2 corrections/feature)

**Source**: [Jon Williams LinkedIn](https://www.linkedin.com/posts/thatjonwilliams_ive-been-using-cursor-for-six-months-now-activity-7424481861802033153-k8bu)

{{< pagebreak >}}

# Agent Teams: Multi-Instance Coordination

**Status**: Experimental (v2.1.32+). Choose an available model per teammate; Opus is optional.

## Lead-Teammate Architecture

Multiple Claude instances work in parallel on a shared codebase, each handling a distinct part of the work.

**Coordination**:
- A shared task list under `~/.claude/tasks/<team-name>/`, with file locking for task claims
- Peer-to-peer messaging (mailbox system)
- Team lead synthesizes findings

**Activation**:
```bash
export CLAUDE_CODE_EXPERIMENTAL_AGENT_TEAMS=1
# Or in ~/.claude/settings.json
```

> ⚠️ **Known risks before deploying:**
> - **Merge conflicts**: multiple agents modifying the same files → prefer modular architecture with clear per-agent file ownership
> - **Additional cost**: each agent loads context and makes model calls. Measure aggregate input/output tokens and coordination overhead; agent count alone does not establish a run price.
> - **Coordination overhead**: add agents only for independently useful work; a fixed five-agent ceiling is not a product limit.
> - **Shared-file conflicts**: task-claim locking does not protect source files. Give agents separate file ownership or worktrees.
>
> **Mitigation:** Start with 2 agents (lead + 1 specialist), read-heavy tasks only, budget warning via `claude_budget_check`; use a billing or gateway control for an enforced cap. → See **#6 Privacy & Compliance** (`06-privacy.qmd`) for data implications of multi-agent sessions.

```
Multi-Agent Review Sequence
────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Agent Lead          Agent Security    Agent API    Agent Frontend
     │                    │               │              │
     │── Scan vulns ──────>               │              │
     │   (read-only)       │               │              │
     │── Review endpoints ────────────────>              │
     │   (read-only)       │               │              │
     │── Check UI + a11y ──────────────────────────────>│
     │   (read-only)       │               │              │
     │<── Security report ─┤               │              │
     │<── API design report────────────────┤              │
     │<── Accessibility report─────────────────────────── │
     │                    │               │              │
     │ [Consolidated synthesis]           │              │
────────────────────────────────────────────────────
```

## Team Use Cases

::: {.callout-note title="Scenario: Multi-Layer Review, Fountain (workforce management)"}
**Context**: Fountain, a workforce management platform for logistics, uses multi-agent Claude Code for candidate screening (not code review).

**Approach**: 3 specialized agents in parallel (security, API design, frontend accessibility), each in read-only mode on the PR, with a lead agent consolidating reports.

**Result**: 50% reduction in candidate screening time, 40% faster developer onboarding (source: anthropic.com).

**Caveat**: These gains apply to a specific domain (workforce management), not general-purpose development. Direct transfer to a typical product team is not guaranteed.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Scenario: Full Dev Lifecycle, CRED (fintech)"}
**Context**: CRED, an Indian fintech company, integrates Claude Code across the full development cycle, from spec to deployment.

**Result**: Feature delivery time cut in half (source: planify.in, Sept. 2025).

**Caveat**: The "delivery time" metric covers the full pipeline (spec, dev, review, deploy). Attribution to Claude Code alone vs. overall process improvement is not isolated.
:::

## When to Deploy as a Team

| Criterion | Teams ✅ | Single ❌ |
|-----------|----------|-----------|
| **Task type** | Read-heavy (review, analysis) | Write-heavy (refactoring shared files) |
| **Budget** | >$300/month | <$100/month |
| **Complexity** | >5 files, multi-layers | <5 files |
| **Architecture** | Modular (clear boundaries) | Monolithic |

**Anti-pattern** : >5 agents = coordination overhead > productivity

The most frequent trap is deploying write-mode agents on shared files. Merge conflicts between agents are silent: no "resolve conflict" dialog, just a commit that overwrites another agent's work. Read-heavy tasks (review, analysis, audit) are the natural playground for multi-agent setups.

## Dedicated Reviewer Teammate (v3.38.0)

Illustrative pattern: dedicate one Opus 5.5 reviewer to a bounded group of implementation agents. Explicitly configure how task completion triggers review; measure review capacity rather than treating a fixed staffing ratio as validated.

**Architecture**:

```
TaskCompleted → configured reviewer (Opus 5.5, read-only)
  → Checks coherence + quality
  → Posts report to .claude/reviews/
  → Lead agent decides next step (merge / rework / escalate)
```

**Why read-only**: the reviewer never writes code; it evaluates. Separating evaluation from implementation reduces confirmation bias and correction loops.

**1:4 ratio**: beyond this, the reviewer becomes a bottleneck. Below 4 active agents, a manual review is usually faster.

## Loop Guardrails (v3.38.0)

For unattended CI/CD workflows, agent loops without explicit exit conditions can burn significant budget. Three recommended guardrails:

Add to each teammate's brief:

> Maximum 8 attempts on any single failing task. Before retrying, answer: what specifically failed? What one change would fix it? If still blocked after 8 attempts, stop and report to team lead.

This is not a native `settings.json` key, it's prompt text in the task brief.

| Guardrail | Effect | Recommended value |
|-----------|--------|------------------|
| Attempt limit | Forced stop after N iterations | 8 (adjustable per task type) |
| Reflection prompt | Agent evaluates its own progress before continuing | Mandatory in CI |
| Kill / reassign | Exit criteria if agent is looping | Define per task type |

**Kill/reassign criteria**: if 3 consecutive iterations produce the same output, or cost exceeds the task budget, the task is reassigned or abandoned.

## `${CLAUDE_EFFORT}` in Team Skills (v2.1.120)

Skills can reference the current effort level via `${CLAUDE_EFFORT}`. In a team context, this standardizes skills while adapting them to the execution context:

```yaml
---
name: code-review
---
Perform a code review at effort level ${CLAUDE_EFFORT}.
If xhigh: deep security + architecture analysis.
If low: quick style and obvious bug check.
```

Useful for teams that alternate between quick reviews (frequent commits) and thorough reviews (critical PRs).

## Background Agents Workflow

**Use case**: Long-running tests, CI/CD builds without blocking your session.

```bash
# Prefix with & for background execution
& "run full test suite"
# Or use Ctrl+B to move a task to background
# /tasks to view running tasks
```

**Difference**:
- `&` prefix / `Ctrl+B` → async, non-blocking
- Task tool → sync, blocks until summary

# Costs and Optimization

## Pricing by Model

Choose models from measured task outcomes and total cost. A team can explicitly route bounded work to Haiku or Sonnet and compare Opus or Fable for harder work. This routing policy is distinct from the account's default model.

| Model | Input | Output | Usage Type |
|-------|-------|--------|------------|
| **Haiku 4.5** | $1/1M | $5/1M | Bounded tasks; 200K context, no effort parameter |
| **Sonnet 5** | $2/1M | $10/1M | Explicit routing choice, native 1M context |
| **Opus 5.5** | $4/1M | $20/1M | Current direct-service default, native 1M context |
| **Fable 5.1** | $10/1M | $50/1M | Available on eligible accounts, native 1M context |

Standard direct-API rates above were verified for the guide on September 24, 2026. Sonnet 5 remains $2/$10 after the launch promotion. Opus 5.5 is the direct-service default; organization policy and provider aliases can differ. Fast mode and caching use separate rates.

## Cost-Saving Strategies

### 1. Model Switching

```bash
/model haiku    # Simple tasks
/model sonnet   # Development
/model opus     # Complex architecture
```

### 2. OpusPlan Pattern

OpusPlan uses Opus for planning and Sonnet for implementation. Selecting Haiku is a separate routing choice.

```bash
/model opusplan
> Plan the refactoring of the auth system
# Opus plans, Sonnet implements
```

### 3. Context Management

| Zone | Context | Action |
|------|---------|--------|
| Green | 0-50% | Work freely |
| Yellow | 50-70% | Prepare: be selective, avoid large file reads |
| Orange | 70%+ | Act: `/compact` to free up space |
| Red | 90%+ | Critical: `/clear` (context loss) |

### 4. Budget Alerts

```bash
# In ~/.zshrc
claude_budget_check() {
  local cost=$(session-stats.sh --json | jq -r '.summary.estimated_cost.total')
  local threshold=5.00  # $5/day

  if (( $(echo "$cost > $threshold" | bc -l) )); then
    echo "⚠️  Claude spend: \$$cost (threshold: \$$threshold)"
  fi
}

claude_budget_check  # On shell startup
```

This shell heuristic works for a solo dev but doesn't stop overspend before it happens, it only reports it after the fact. For team-wide enforcement, route Claude Code through a gateway instead: `guide/ops/api-gateway.md` §3 documents virtual keys with hard budget caps per developer or per team, returning a 429 once the cap is hit rather than surfacing a warning after the invoice lands. §4 of the same guide covers model allowlists, restricting which models a given key can call, useful for capping junior devs to Sonnet while leads keep Opus access.

## Team Budget

| Profile | Suggested budget/day | Notes |
|---------|----------------------|-------|
| Junior dev | $5-10 | Learning |
| Senior dev | $10-20 | Productivity |
| Tech Lead | $15-30 | Reviews + arch |
| Team (10 devs) | $100-200 | Aggregated |

These illustrative ranges assume an explicit Sonnet routing policy with occasional Opus switches for architecture tasks; they are not measured current-model budgets. In practice, cost varies significantly by usage pattern: a dev doing TDD in loops consumes 3-5x more than one using Claude Code for occasional reviews. The `session-summary.sh` hook (Observability section) lets each dev calibrate their own budget on real data rather than estimates.

> 📖 **Go further:** [§9.13 Cost Optimization Strategies](https://github.com/FlorianBruniaux/claude-code-ultimate-guide/blob/main/guide/ultimate-guide.md#913-cost-optimization-strategies): OpusPlan, Haiku routing, budget alerts

# Governance

## Enterprise Features (Claude for Teams)

**Available**: Anthropic Teams/Enterprise plans

Propagating configuration to a team no longer means guessing at undocumented admin console fields. Three concrete mechanisms now cover this: a shared `.claude/settings.json` committed to the repo (covered earlier in this whitepaper), a `CLAUDE.md` hierarchy that lets org-wide, project-wide, and personal rules layer without conflict, and the Anthropic Team/Enterprise admin console itself for org-level policy that can't live in a repo (SSO enforcement, seat management, usage caps). See `guide/security/enterprise-governance.md` §2.3 for the full mechanics of each path.

**Capabilities**:

- **SSO/SAML**: Okta, Google Workspace, Azure AD integration
- **Admin console**: Centralized user, permission, and quota management
- **Usage analytics**: Team-wide token consumption dashboards
- **Data retention policies**: Session storage control (GDPR compliance)
- **API key rotation**: Automated secret management
- **Audit logs**: Compliance trail (SOC 2, ISO 27001)

**Deployment**: Configure organization identity, seats and audit capabilities through the supported administration interface. Deploy enforced client policies through managed settings. A user `settings.json` object named `organization` does not configure SSO or enable audit logs. See [managed settings](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/settings#settings-files-and-who-they-affect).

**Use case** : Teams >50 devs, compliance-driven industries (finance, healthcare)

## Shared vs Personal Separation

The boundary between shared and personal configuration is a frequent source of confusion on teams. The rule is simple: anything that affects project behavior (tests, conventions, security hooks) goes in the repo, anything related to individual comfort (preferred model, response language) stays local.

| Shared (repo) | Personal (~/.claude) |
|----------------|----------------------|
| Test/lint commands | Model preferences |
| Project conventions | Personal agents |
| Commit format | Default flags |
| Security hooks | Optional extensions |

## Audit Trail

### Logging Configuration

→ See Observability section configuration

### Team Aggregation

```bash
# Daily sync to S3
aws s3 sync ~/.claude/logs/ s3://company-claude-logs/$(whoami)/

# Aggregate all team logs
aws s3 sync s3://company-claude-logs/ /tmp/team-logs/

# Analyze
cat /tmp/team-logs/*/activity-*.jsonl | \
  jq -s 'group_by(.project) | map({
    project: .[0].project,
    total_tokens: [.[].tokens.total] | add
  })'
```

This S3/jq pipeline is a reasonable starting point but stays manual: someone has to run the sync, write the query, refresh the dashboard. `guide/ops/observability.md` §10 documents two more current paths: routing through the LiteLLM Gateway (recommended, gives you usage dashboards for free as a side effect of the budget-cap setup above) or shipping session JSONL to Loki with an OTel Collector for Tempo traces and Prometheus/Grafana queries. Either replaces this ad-hoc script with a queryable, always-on aggregation.

### Log Rotation

```bash
# Clean logs older than 30 days
find ~/.claude/logs -name "*.jsonl" -mtime +30 -delete
```

::: {.callout-tip title="Memo: First Month Onboarding"}
**What**: Deploy Claude Code across an existing team without breaking the established workflow.

**When**: Week 1 = minimal config + 2 champions. Week 2-3 = expansion. Week 4 = review.

**How**: Turnkey Quickstart (15-line CLAUDE.md) → live demo at standup → open PRs for additions → session-summary.sh for cost visibility.

**Verify**: After 1 month, how many devs actively use it? Has the CLAUDE.md grown organically? Are costs within the budgeted range?
:::

## Onboarding a New Team Member

The goal: a new dev fully operational with Claude Code in under an hour, without needing someone available to walk them through it.

::: {.callout-tip title="Claude Code onboarding checklist: New member"}
**Estimated time: 45 minutes**

**Step 1: Installation (10 min)**

1. Use the [supported installation instructions](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/setup), preferably the native installer
2. Run `claude` and authenticate using the organization-approved subscription, Console or provider path
3. Verify: `claude --version`

**Step 2: Project config (15 min)**

4. Read `CLAUDE.md` at the root (project conventions, stack, commands)
5. If a `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md.example` template is provided in the repo: copy it to `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md` and adjust language and style preferences
6. Open `.claude/settings.json` to understand which hooks are active

**Step 3: First run (20 min)**

7. Open the project in terminal
8. `claude` → start a session
9. Test: *"Explain the architecture of this project"* (validates that `CLAUDE.md` is being read)
10. Inspect rules with `/permissions`, registered hooks with `/hooks`, and loaded settings sources with `/status`
11. Test a hook: modify a file and verify no blocking hook fires unexpectedly
:::

**What the repo must provide** to make this onboarding self-service:

| File | Expected content |
|------|-----------------|
| `CLAUDE.md` (root) | Stack, test/lint commands, main conventions |
| `.claude/settings.json` | Active hooks (committed, therefore visible) |
| `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md.example` | Personal config template with comments |
| `CONTRIBUTING.md` or `README.md` | Link to these 3 files + "Claude Code ready" mention |

::: {.callout-note title="Sharing strategies: comparison"}
| Mechanism | Advantages | Drawbacks | Use case |
|-----------|-----------|-----------|----------|
| **Committed CLAUDE.md** | Visible, versioned, reviewable in PRs | Text only, no conditional logic | Conventions, stack, commands |
| **Committed `.claude/settings.json`** | Hooks shared automatically, structured JSON | Overwrites user settings on shared keys | Security hooks, tool allowlists |
| **Git hooks (pre-commit)** | Independent of Claude Code, universal | Only applies to commits, not sessions | Lint, format, secrets scan |
| **`~/.claude/CLAUDE.md` (personal)** | Additions without team impact | Not shared, invisible to others | Preferences, language, shortcuts |

**Recommendation**: Start with committed `CLAUDE.md` + `settings.json`. Layer in existing project Git hooks; avoid duplicating in Claude Code what is already enforced by pre-commit.
:::
